Indeed, the absence of a definition strongly indicates a desire for flexibility in approach that a board of experts such as the Commission could give through interpretation of the term as the transportation industry evolved. Freight Forwarders Institute v. United States, 409 F. Supp. at 703.
The early cases construing the scope of the commercial zone exemption employed a test which distinguished between "intraterminal" and "intercity or intercommunity" operations and spoke of local operations within a "single community." The Commission drew commercial zone boundaries to reflect the geographic extent of intraterminal motor freight movements at cities. Only local operations within a single community were considered within the purview of the section 203(b)(8) exemption. See, St. Louis, Mo.-East St. Louis, Ill., Commercial Zone, 1 M.C.C. at 661, New York, N.Y., Commercial Zone, 1 M.C.C. at 671, Chicago, Ill., Commercial Zone, 1 M.C.C. at 677, and New York, N.Y., Commercial Zone, 2 M.C.C. at 192. The "intraterminal" test has its conceptual roots in the notion of a railroad terminal area - the area for which a single rate or tariff applied for purposes of interterminal or intercity rail transport. In the early days of motor carrier regulation, the "intraterminal" idea served to describe adequately the extent of local operations.
